lesson.title: x Equals a Constant: The Line That Breaks the Slope Formula
lesson.summary: A vertical line is the graph of every point sharing the same x-coordinate, described by x equals a constant and carrying an undefined slope rather than a numeric one.
lesson.body:
A vertical line is the mirror image of a horizontal line, and it is the direct picture of undefined slope. Every point on a vertical line shares the exact same x-coordinate, while the y-coordinate is free to be anything at all. Because there is no x-term that changes, the equation describing a vertical line needs no y at all, it is simply x equals some constant number, often written x = c.

Consider the equation x equals negative 2. Some points that satisfy this equation are (negative 2, 5), (negative 2, 0), and (negative 2, negative 3). The y-coordinates here are all different, 5, 0, and negative 3, while every x-coordinate stays fixed at negative 2. Plotting these points and connecting them produces a perfectly straight vertical line running straight up and down through x equals negative 2. Try computing the slope between two of these points, say (negative 2, 5) and (negative 2, 0): m equals (0 minus 5) divided by (negative 2 minus negative 2), which is negative 5 divided by 0. Division by 0 is not defined, so the slope of a vertical line is always undefined, matching exactly what you already learned about undefined slope.

This undefined slope is also why a vertical line cannot be written in slope-intercept form or point-slope form, since both of those forms require plugging in a numeric value for m, and no such value exists here. Standard form, A x plus B y equals C, can still describe a vertical line by simply setting B = 0, for example x equals negative 2 can be written as 1 times x plus 0 times y equals negative 2, though in practice it is almost always left in the simple form x = c.

A vertical line has no y-intercept unless the constant itself is 0, in which case the line is x equals 0, which is the y-axis itself. For any other constant, such as x equals negative 2, the line never crosses the y-axis at all, because the x-coordinate is locked at negative 2 and can never become 0. It does, however, cross the x-axis exactly once, at the point (negative 2, 0), since every value of y is allowed.

A useful memory trick is that a vertical line looks like the letter x standing straight up, so its equation is x equals a number, while a horizontal line lies flat like the letter y written sideways along the page, so its equation is y equals a number. Whenever an equation contains only x, with no y term at all, the graph of a line is vertical, and the slope is undefined rather than 0.

Graphing x equals negative 2 is just as quick as graphing a horizontal line, once you know the pattern. Draw a single straight line running straight up and down through negative 2 on the x-axis, extending as far up and down as the graph allows. Every point on that line automatically satisfies the equation, since x is locked at negative 2 while y is free to take any value. It is worth pausing on why a vertical line is not itself a function, even though it is a perfectly valid graph of a line: a function requires each input x to produce exactly one output y, but on the line x equals negative 2, the single input negative 2 corresponds to infinitely many outputs, every y-value at once. This is the one major place where the graph of a line and the graph of a function part ways, and it is a direct consequence of the same undefined slope that makes the vertical line special in the first place.
